title: Liberties
summary: Liberties are the empty points adjacent to a stone or group. Counting liberties is the foundation of every Go tactic.

steps.title: A single stone has 4 liberties
steps.body: A stone in the center of the board has 4 liberties: up, down, left, right. Diagonal points are NOT liberties — only orthogonal ones count.

steps.title: Edge stones have 3 liberties
steps.body: On the edge, the board boundary blocks one liberty. The black stone here has 3: left, right, and down.

steps.title: Corner stones have only 2 liberties
steps.body: The corner stone has just 2 liberties — right and down. This is why corner stones are easier to attack but also easier to defend efficiently.

steps.title: Connected stones share liberties
steps.body: Two black stones connected vertically form one group with 6 liberties total. The point between them is shared, not counted twice. Larger groups can have more liberties — but they can also be captured all at once.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: Test what you've learned about liberties.
steps.quizQuestion: How many liberties does a single stone in the corner have?
steps.quizExplanation: Two of the four orthogonal directions are blocked by the board edge, leaving just 2 liberties. That's why corner stones are easier to attack.

title: Capturing & Atari
summary: When a stone or group runs out of liberties it is captured and removed from the board. Atari is the warning state — one liberty left.

steps.title: White is in atari
steps.body: The white stone has only one liberty left — the empty point below it. Tap that point to capture white. (This state is called atari — one move from capture.)

steps.title: Black captures
steps.body: Black plays the last liberty. The white stone has zero liberties and is removed from the board immediately. Black's capture count goes up by 1.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: Let's make sure 'atari' is locked in.
steps.quizQuestion: What does it mean when a group is in atari?
quizChoices: It has exactly one liberty left
It is connected to another group
steps.quizExplanation: Atari is the warning state — the group has one liberty left, so the opponent can capture next turn unless you defend or extend.

title: The Ko Rule
summary: Ko prevents an infinite loop of capture-and-recapture. After capturing in a ko, you must play elsewhere before you can recapture.

steps.title: A ko shape
steps.body: The empty point at the center is a 'ko' — whoever plays there captures the opposing stone next to it. Tap the ko point to take the white stone. (Without the ko rule, the game could loop forever.)

steps.title: Black takes the ko
steps.body: Black plays at the center, capturing the white stone that was at (2,2). White is NOT allowed to immediately retake this capture; they must play elsewhere first.

steps.title: Ko threats
steps.body: Strong play in a ko involves 'ko threats' — moves elsewhere on the board that the opponent must answer. Press Play to watch a complete ko exchange.

demoMoves.caption: White plays a ko threat on the other side of the board.
Black answers the threat to protect against the threatened damage.
Now the position has changed — White retakes the ko, capturing the black stone.
The captured black stone is removed from the board. The ko swings back to White.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: How well do you remember the Ko rule?
steps.quizQuestion: Right after capturing a stone in a ko, when can you take that same point again?
quizChoices: After playing at least one move elsewhere
You can never retake a ko
steps.quizExplanation: The Ko rule forbids immediately recreating the previous board position. You must play another move first — usually a ko threat — before retaking.

title: Eyes and Life
summary: A group with two separate eyes (empty interior points completely surrounded by your stones) cannot be captured. This is the most important survival concept in Go.

steps.title: One eye is not enough
steps.body: This black group has only one eye (the empty point at (2,2)) and one outside liberty. White can fill the outside liberty, then play inside the eye, and black is captured. One eye dies.

steps.title: Two eyes — alive forever
steps.body: Now the group has TWO separate eyes — at (2,2) and (2,4). White cannot fill either: any white stone played in an eye has zero liberties (suicide). Two eyes = unconditional life. The proverb: 'Two eyes live, one eye dies.'

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: The single most important concept in life-and-death.
steps.quizQuestion: How many real eyes does a group need to be unconditionally alive?
steps.quizExplanation: Two separate real eyes make a group unkillable: the opponent can't fill both at once without playing a suicidal stone.

title: False Eyes
summary: Not every empty interior point is a real eye. A 'false eye' looks like an eye but collapses when its diagonal stones are captured.

steps.title: A real eye in the center
steps.body: All four orthogonal AND all four diagonal points around the empty space are black. This is a real eye — it cannot be invaded.

steps.title: A false eye on the edge
steps.body: The empty point at (0,1) looks like an eye — both orthogonal neighbors are black. But the corner diagonal at (1,0) is empty. If white can capture stones around the diagonal, the 'eye' falls apart. False eyes are why edge and corner shapes need extra attention.

steps.title: The diagonal rule
steps.body: The shorthand: for an interior eye, you usually need 3 of the 4 diagonals to be your color (all 4 in the corner; 2 of 2 on the edge). If too many diagonals are missing or the opponent's, you have a false eye and should treat it as if it were filled.

title: Ladders (Shicho)
summary: A ladder is a sequence of moves that chases a stone in a zigzag path toward the edge. Master this basic capturing technique.

steps.title: What is a ladder?
steps.body: A ladder (shicho) traps a stone by putting it in atari repeatedly. White at (5,3) has exactly one liberty — north at (4,3). Black gives atari, White runs, Black gives atari again. Press Play to watch the zigzag chase.

demoMoves.caption: White runs north — the only liberty.
Black gives atari from above-right — one liberty left: west.
White flees west — the zigzag begins.
Atari from the left — Black stays one step ahead.
White runs north again.
Atari from above — the zigzag continues toward the corner.

steps.title: The zigzag chase
steps.body: After two escapes the White chain stretches from (5,3) through (4,3) to (4,2) — three stones, all connected. White still has only one liberty at (3,2). The direction alternates: north, west, north, west — a diagonal zigzag toward the corner.

steps.title: The edge is the wall
steps.body: The full seven-stone White chain has been chased to the left edge. Only one liberty remains at (1,0). The board boundary acts as an extra wall — White cannot escape. Press Play to see Black capture.

demoMoves.caption: Black fills the last liberty — all seven White stones are captured!

steps.title: Ladder breakers
steps.body: A 'ladder breaker' is a White stone placed in the path of the ladder. When the fleeing chain reaches it, the two White groups merge and gain extra liberties — White escapes! Press Play to see the ladder fail.

demoMoves.caption: White runs north — same start as before.
Black gives atari.
White flees west.
Atari again.
White runs north.
Black gives atari — but the breaker at (2,1) is in White's next escape point!
White connects to the breaker — three liberties now. The ladder fails!

steps.title: Read before you play
steps.body: Before starting a ladder, trace the full diagonal path in your mind all the way to the edge. If a friendly stone sits anywhere along that path — a ladder breaker! — the ladder will fail and you will lose your chasing stones instead. Always read ahead.

title: Atari & Escape
summary: Atari means your group has only one liberty left. Learn to recognise and respond to atari threats — both giving and escaping them.

steps.title: What is atari?
steps.body: White at (3,3) has four Black stones around it — only one liberty remains above at (2,3). This is atari: one move away from capture. In Japanese Go, the attacker says 'atari' to warn the opponent.

steps.title: Escaping atari — extend
steps.body: White at (3,2) is in atari — its only liberty is to the east. Press Play to see the escape and what happens next.

demoMoves.caption: White extends east — the group now has three new liberties.
Black chases — places a stone east of the running group.
White runs again — but each step uses precious liberties.
Black gives atari from the north. White is in trouble again.

steps.title: Escaping atari — capture the attacker
steps.body: Another escape: if the attacking stone is isolated, put it in atari instead! White plays at (4,3), reducing Black(3,3) to atari. If Black doesn't respond, White captures. This counter-attack is called a 'snapback' set-up.

steps.title: Atari is a warning, not a capture
steps.body: Remember: atari is not capture — it's one move away from capture. The group still has exactly one liberty. Always respond to atari unless you have a deliberate reason not to (e.g., a ko threat or a sacrifice).

title: Connecting Stones
summary: Connected stones share liberties and are much harder to capture. Learn the key connection shapes: solid, diagonal, one-point jump, knight's move.

steps.title: Solid connection
steps.body: The simplest connection: two stones sharing a side. Black at (3,2) and (3,3) are solidly connected — they count as one group with shared liberties. An opponent cannot cut between them.

steps.title: Tiger's mouth (hanging connection)
steps.body: Three stones forming a 'mouth' shape. Press Play to see what happens when an opponent tries to cut.

demoMoves.caption: White tries to cut by playing inside the mouth.
Self-atari — White has zero liberties and is captured immediately. The mouth holds firm.

steps.title: Bamboo joint
steps.body: Four stones in a 2×2-with-gaps pattern. The two empty interior points mean an opponent can never cut because playing on either point causes immediate capture. Bamboo joints are very common in real games.

steps.title: One-point jump (tobi)
steps.body: Two stones with one empty point between them. This is NOT solidly connected — an opponent can play the middle point to cut. However, the one-point jump is fast and efficient; a cut can often be handled tactically.

title: Territory Basics
summary: Go is ultimately about territory — empty points enclosed by your stones. Learn how territory is formed, counted, and contested.

steps.title: What counts as territory?
steps.body: Territory is the set of empty points entirely enclosed by one player's stones. The four empty points inside the Black rectangle all count as Black territory — 4 points. No white stones can enter safely.

steps.title: Territory vs. influence
steps.body: Black controls the top-left corner and the left edge, but the interior is large and open — it is influence (moyo), not yet territory. Influence can become territory if Black seals it off, or white can invade and reduce it.

steps.title: Counting at game end
steps.body: At game end, count territory (empty points surrounded) minus captured prisoners. Black has 1 point (top-left interior), White has 2 (top-right interior). The rest is dame (neutral). Japanese rules count territory + prisoners; Chinese rules count stones + territory.

title: Opening Principles
summary: The opening (fuseki) sets the direction of the whole game. Learn the classic priorities: corners, sides, then centre.

steps.title: Corners first
steps.body: Corners are the most efficient place to start. With only two sides of the board to defend, you can claim large territory with fewer stones. The 3-3, 3-4 (komoku), and 4-4 (star point / hoshi) are common first moves.

steps.title: Sides second
steps.body: Once corners are claimed, expand to the sides. A stone on the side (third or fourth line) can develop territory efficiently using the edge as a natural boundary. Connecting corners via side moves builds large frameworks.

steps.title: Centre last
steps.body: Centre stones have influence in all directions but no edge to lean on — they need more stones to build enclosed territory. Play centre only after securing corners and sides, or as a response to opponent's framework. 'A game begins at the corners' is a fundamental Go proverb.
